Radar absorbing materials are used as the main components in the creation of electromagnetic wave absorbers, which are used for the equipment of anechoic chambers.

Resonant radar absorbing materials provide partial neutralization of radiation reflected from the surface of the absorber, where the thickness of the absorber is equal to one quarter of the wavelength of the radiation.
Nickel ferrites are used mainly in the ranges of mile-and centimeter waves, have high values of saturation magnetization and high thermal stability, but have the disadvantage of high initial losses.
Magnetic ferrites are used in the middle part of the centimeter range, have low magnetic saturation, and the main drawback is low thermal stability.
Metal screens at almost acceptable thickness provide good shielding efficiency at all frequencies of the radio band, with efficiency increasing with frequency.

Non-resonant bulk radar absorbing materials absorb most of the energy supplied to the approach and possible reflection of the wave from the metal back plate, using both dielectric and magnetic losses.

Radar absorbing materials based on metamaterials have the ability to absorb electromagnetic waves at plasma resonance frequencies, due to the resonance interaction of the electromagnetic wave propagating in a heterogeneous medium.
Metamaterials can have both negative magnetic permeability and electrical susceptibility, resulting in electromagnetic waves with opposite phase and group velocities.

An example of a technical solution for a two-dimensional microwave absorber based on metamaterial is a dielectric layer with SRR cells applied, providing an absorption level of not less than 80% at EMV incidence angles from 0 to 50 degrees at a frequency of 9.5 GHz.
